title: Persistent communicating leak after collection control
fairness: Report scope: all 12 current executable candidate nodes, including the four pass-preserved versions, were independently assessed from their current presentation, update, exhibit, task, option labels and explanation. The 17 kept original records, 18 retired/replacement source records, seven parked attempts and withheld teaching points were noted but not scored. Historical versions and author self-assessments were not evidence for these verdicts. This is an offline editorial review, not fresh source verification or Melissa Rowland's clinical approval; every clinical draft remains needs_clinician_review. Difficulty and highYield are qualitative judgments, not measured performance or verified examination-frequency claims. No statistics items are present.

ERCP with transpapillary plastic stenting is the defensible best offered intervention: the resident must infer a communicating stump leak from the duct map and then distinguish ongoing leakage needing diversion from a collection needing new drainage. The contracting cavity changes the interpretation of continued drain output.

The alternatives are named procedures at the same decision stage. The functioning catheter and preserved duct passage are necessary observations, not pre-answer declarations that the competing procedures are wrong. No decisive grammar, length, absolute, diagnosis-label or nonmedical wording shortcut was identified.

The 46-year-old named woman's clinic visit and retrospective hospital decision are coherent. The task identifies the intervention decision, and all required history is present without a previous node. Minor-leak diversion versus major injury or failed collection control is high-yield general-surgery material. No confident clinical inaccuracy was identified.

title: Primary-lesion sampling during curative perihilar evaluation
fairness: ERCP brushings with intraductal forceps biopsies is the best offered route. The resident must interpret the confluence-centered lesion and then apply the primary-tumor sampling boundary while a transplant pathway remains possible. The primary target is explicit; the item does not accidentally prohibit EUS sampling of a different staging target.

The potential transplant pathway is decision-critical rather than gratuitous permission. All options obtain tissue from the primary lesion. The ERCP label contains two sampling methods while the others name needle biopsy, but choosing it on that superficial difference alone is not a reliable shortcut; the clinically meaningful distinction remains the sampling route.

The named 58-year-old woman's referral supplies a complete standalone decision. There is no prior feedback supplying the answer. Avoiding a sampling route that can compromise a curative pathway is a high-yield oncologic principle. No confident clinical inaccuracy was identified; actual transplant eligibility and diagnostic yield are appropriately not asserted.

title: Postcholecystectomy collection with unresolved arterial perfusion
fairness: Multiphasic contrast-enhanced abdominal CT is the best offered next study. The resident must recognize that non-established hepatic arterial flow raises a question beyond detecting bile leakage, then choose an examination that can assess the vasculature and collection. The MR cholangiography distractor remains tempting because duct dilation and bile drainage are also present.

Doppler nonvisualization is not presented as proof of arterial transection, and the explanation does not claim CT replaces all subsequent duct mapping. The three choices are parallel investigations. No task word uniquely repeats the key, and the presentation does not name the desired modality.

The named 51-year-old woman's stable hospital imaging stage is distinguishable from her later clinic review. The task stands alone with the supplied presentation. Recognition and assessment of combined biliary and vascular injury are high-yield; no confident clinical inaccuracy was identified.

title: Rescue drainage after inaccessible papilla in malignant obstruction
fairness: EUS-guided biliary drainage is a defensible preferred offered approach in this expert-center setting after failed papillary access. Percutaneous drainage is a credible alternative rather than an inherently incorrect treatment; the single-best ranking depends on the stated expertise and feasible access, not on a universal prohibition of percutaneous drainage.

The resident must distinguish failure to reach the papilla from a generic failed ERCP, then apply the accessible stomach and dilated left ducts to an alternative drainage route. The advanced-anatomy component adds reasoning to a high-yield palliative obstruction decision.

Expertise is explicitly supplied for both EUS and percutaneous drainage, so availability does not name the key. The stomach and duct observations require clinical interpretation rather than word matching. Options are comparably concise procedures, and no decisive nonmedical cue was identified.

The update follows the named 71-year-old man's drainage plan coherently and supplies the entire failed-procedure result. Although this is now one executable node, the chronological update remains self-contained and no earlier answer is needed. No confident clinical inaccuracy was identified.
suggestions: Optional precision: ask which rescue procedure is preferred as the next intervention, rather than which procedure the team should discuss. The present single-best-answer context supports a preference, but both endoscopic and percutaneous options can legitimately be discussed.

In feedback, make the conditional preference over percutaneous drainage explicit while retaining the existing statement that percutaneous drainage remains appropriate when EUS access or expertise is unsuitable. Any added comparative outcome claim needs verified support.

title: Drainage route for a recurrent contained postoperative collection

cues.phrase: An anterior percutaneous path enters the pocket without crossing bowel or pleura.
cues.why: The exhibit already describes the successful route using the same distinctive word as 'Percutaneous image-guided catheter drainage'. No equivalent access anatomy is supplied for the EUS competitor. A nonmedical reader can favor the explicitly available named route. Access information is necessary, but this wording and option set largely perform the route-selection inference.

cues.phrase: One encapsulated subhepatic pocket; no free fluid elsewhere in the abdomen.
cues.why: Together with 'Stable blood pressure' and 'without rigidity', this makes the operative alternative a conspicuous escalation after the named percutaneous route is already supplied. These are valid safety findings to retain; the weakness is that the remaining competition does not turn them into a difficult decision.

fairness: Percutaneous catheter drainage is the defensible best offered initial procedure for this localized collection with a displaced catheter and an accessible route. No confident clinical inaccuracy was identified. The problem is insufficient discrimination, not that source control should be delayed.

The stopped drain and catheter outside the pocket establish a straightforward mechanical failure. Choosing the explicitly described access route then requires little additional consequential inference. EUS drainage is not established as impossible, but its relationship to the stomach or duodenum is not described, so it is a weak competitor rather than a demonstrated equally plausible approach.

The named 46-year-old woman's prior leak treatment, deterioration, fluids and antibiotics are coherent. This standalone candidate does not require the previous communicating-leak question or its feedback. Source control and recognition of failed drainage are high yield; advanced EUS collection drainage should not be used merely to make the option list sound difficult.
suggestions: Rebuild the competition around a real residual source-control decision. If comparing percutaneous and transluminal routes, supply the relevant observed collection relationships for both and a supported patient-specific reason for preferring one; avoid announcing the preferred access route in the exhibit.
Keep the displaced catheter, physiology and distribution findings. Do not manufacture difficulty by hiding peritonitis findings or the information needed to choose safe drainage.

If the intended objective remains basic recognition of an accessible undrained biloma, seek explicit acceptance of an easy safety/recognition item instead of calling this exact version a difficult two-step resident item.

title: Interim proximal decompression after major duct injury
fairness: Percutaneous transhepatic biliary drainage is the best offered interim intervention. The resident must distinguish the drained extrabiliary cavity from the dilated proximal duct systems and then recognize that the failed wire passage prevents routine transpapillary treatment from reaching the relevant system.

Rigors, jaundice and rising bilirubin supply the clinical reason to decompress rather than simply observe a controlled cavity. Fluids, antibiotics and HPB involvement are shared context, so the drainage choice does not omit resuscitation or claim to replace definitive specialist repair.

The collapsed cavity and abrupt duct end legitimately distinguish the competitors; neither finding names transhepatic drainage in advance. All options are specific drainage procedures, with two percutaneous choices preventing a simple route-word shortcut. The question asks for interim care rather than an unsupported universal reconstruction or repair date.

The named 56-year-old woman's hospital timeline is complete without the former companion case. The observation that some proximal contrast enters the drained space does not itself prove adequate decompression of the dilated infected system; the clinical deterioration remains important. Major-duct continuity and proximal source-control decisions are high yield. No confident clinical inaccuracy was identified.

title: Management after fully assessed lamina-propria gallbladder carcinoma

cues.why: In a task asking whether more cancer surgery is needed, this phrasing can suggest oncologic completeness rather than merely that a cholecystectomy occurred. It softly favors surveillance before the learner uses the pathology.

This repeated margin finding, together with 'No residual mass or metastatic disease', creates an all-clear pattern against two further-resection options. The negatives are necessary for fairness, but the option set allows a nonmedical all-clear heuristic and leaves no credible competing specimen interpretation.

fairness: Cancer-team surveillance after cholecystectomy is the defensible best offered plan for the fully represented lesion limited to lamina propria with uninvolved muscle and clear margins. The item correctly distinguishes tissue actually examined from tissue not sampled. No confident clinical inaccuracy was identified.

The expanded adequacy record removes ambiguity but does not by itself create a second consequential decision: every adequacy and clearance finding points the same way. A resident who recalls the T1a management rule can answer directly. Extrahepatic duct resection is a particularly weak competitor with a clear duct margin and no stated duct disease.

The named 43-year-old woman's presentation and constructed pathology exhibit are clear, self-contained and coherent. The T1a treatment boundary is highly testable and worth retaining; the present version is an easy application of that boundary rather than the requested difficult resident reasoning.
suggestions: Use a neutral task such as asking for the next oncologic management plan from the pathology and staging records, without 'completed resection'.

For a routine resident item, create a genuine supported specimen-adequacy or margin-management decision that changes the action, and compare credible plans at that same stage. Do not make the pathology incomplete while continuing to key surveillance as if invasion were excluded.

Alternatively retain the current accurate content under an explicitly accepted easy foundational role. Do not count tissue recognition followed by the memorized T1a rule as two consequential steps merely because the exhibit has several rows.

title: Completion surgery despite negative postoperative imaging
fairness: Completion liver-bed resection with regional lymphadenectomy is the best offered plan for this fit patient with perimuscular invasive disease and no detected metastases. The resident must interpret microscopic depth and then decide that an apparently clear postoperative scan does not remove the indication for completion oncologic surgery.

The negative CT creates a meaningful competing consideration rather than another restatement of favorable pathology. A clear cystic-duct margin distinguishes routine completion surgery from an unsupported duct-directed completion procedure. No confident clinical inaccuracy was identified, and no exact liver-resection volume or lymph-node count is invented.

The options are specific management plans; two are completion operations, so the word 'completion' cannot identify the answer. No decisive wording overlap, unique qualification, absolute or convergence cue was found. Surveillance is a credible error if the learner mistakes absence of macroscopic residual disease for oncologic adequacy.

The named 62-year-old man's pathology, staging and operative fitness are sufficient without an earlier node. This is a classic high-yield incidental gallbladder carcinoma decision. Difficulty is moderate at most, not a stretch-level prediction.

title: Additional clearance for carcinoma in common hepatic duct wall
clarityIssues: The presentation describes a clinic review of a later operation, while the task asks for an 'additional clearance procedure' from specimens including 'Proposed proximal and distal duct-division edges'. It is unclear whether the learner is choosing an intraoperative next step using frozen sections or a subsequent operation after permanent pathology.

The 'Remaining cystic-duct stump, submitted along its length' makes 'Further excision of the remaining cystic-duct stump' awkward: the candidate does not establish what stump tissue is still present to remove.

cues.phrase: Infiltrating adenocarcinoma is present within this wall.
cues.why: This is the sole positive row, explicitly attached to the common hepatic duct wall. The other offered sites are marked 'No carcinoma identified.' Matching the only positive site to duct resection largely answers the item without interpreting a meaningful specimen conflict.

cues.phrase: Proposed proximal and distal duct-division edges, sampled separately
cues.why: This row describes and validates the boundaries of the keyed duct operation before the choice. The supplied operative plan is more specific than the anatomy needed simply to recognize duct-wall involvement.

cues.phrase: Segmental extrahepatic duct resection with hepaticojejunostomy
cues.why: The key is the only option that names both resection and a specific reconstruction; the other options are short further-excision labels for already negative sites. Its greater completeness reinforces the map's direct answer cue.

fairness: Duct resection with reconstruction is the defensible best offered clearance strategy for the documented duct-wall disease. The original negative gallbladder cystic-duct edge and the later positive common hepatic duct wall are different specimens and are not inherently contradictory. No confident clinical inaccuracy is asserted.

The new map resolves every offered site in advance: stump negative, liver-bed margin negative, duct wall positive, proposed duct ends negative. Recognizing that different samples are different does not become a second consequential reasoning step when the alternatives merely resect the two negative locations.

The named 62-year-old man's history supplies the previous margin result, so remembering a prior node is unnecessary. The timeline still needs the explicit decision-stage repair above. Margin-directed surgery and avoiding routine unnecessary duct resection are high-yield concepts, but this version does not meaningfully test that boundary.
suggestions: Specify whether the decision is being made during completion surgery from frozen sections or after surgery from final pathology. State the status of any tissue still in situ without adding an unsupported procedural sequence.

Rebuild the options around clinically credible competing extents or methods of clearance, with the specimen distribution determining which is sufficient. Do not use two known-negative sites as disposable alternatives or pre-label the resection boundaries as the proposed plan.
Make each option comparable in specificity and scope. If reconstruction is included, include the corresponding operative components consistently where appropriate.

Preserve the distinction between the original cut edge and separately sampled retained duct wall. Any new extent-of-resection comparison requires clinician-verified anatomy and claims; do not invent a margin distance or assume sampled negative edges establish all margins.

title: Persistent congenital duct cyst after childhood internal drainage
fairness: Completion cyst excision with hepaticojejunostomy is the best offered long-term plan for discussion. The resident must interpret the childhood operative record as drainage with retained cyst rather than excision, then distinguish definitive management of the retained abnormal duct from simply revising an open anastomosis or accepting prior surgery as adequate.

The patent opening and resolved acute illness are meaningful competing considerations: they make current obstruction or emergency drainage an insufficient explanation for the long-term decision. The absence of a mural nodule does not prove that retaining the cyst is an adequate definitive plan. The explanation appropriately avoids prescribing an exact operative extent in a previously operated field.

The phrase 'no cyst wall was removed' is relevant operative history, not a named recommendation. All options refer to the cyst or its prior operation, so a simple cyst-word match does not identify the key. No decisive nonmedical cue was found.

The named 33-year-old woman's childhood operation, current imaging, treated cholangitis and recovery are chronologically coherent and stand alone. Drainage versus excision of a congenital bile-duct cyst is high-yield general-surgery content. No confident clinical inaccuracy was identified.

title: Additional drainage of an infected territory outside the future remnant
fairness: The right posterior sectoral ducts are the best next biliary target. The learner must interpret the changed sectoral findings as an undrained infectious source and then prioritize source control despite the planned resection of that territory and the functioning left remnant drainage.

The left-versus-right resection plan and the bilirubin response create a genuine competing planning consideration. Both right sectors are undrained, so absence of a stent alone does not select the key. The posterior sector's interval enlargement, debris and adjacent collections distinguish it from unchanged anterior dilation.

The disease is appropriately named because this is a drainage-management task. All choices are parallel anatomic territories. The posterior row has more abnormal findings, but those are the evidence needed to localize the new problem, not an explanatory sentence naming the treatment. No decisive nonmedical wording shortcut was identified beyond reading the clinically relevant abnormality pattern.

The named 58-year-old woman's prior drainage, temporary response and new infection are coherent and fully supplied in this standalone case. Fluids and antibiotics are shared care. The question chooses a biliary territory, not a complete treatment plan for every adjacent collection, and does not overclaim that one drainage route must be used. This is a high-yield source-control principle in a more advanced HPB setting. No confident clinical inaccuracy was identified.

title: Endoscopic treatment of a traversable stricture near the hepatic confluence
fairness: Multiple plastic stents are the defensible preferred offered course for the supplied traversable postoperative stricture very close to the confluence. The resident must use wire passage to establish an endoscopic treatment opportunity and then use the short proximal cuff and branch anatomy to distinguish plastic stenting from a fully covered metal stent.

The benign diagnosis is explicitly an established specialist assessment, so the learner is not asked to infer that negative tissue conclusively excludes cancer. Both endoscopic choices remain credible in benign strictures generally; the question makes anatomy consequential rather than teaching universal plastic-stent superiority.

The 4 mm measurement is treated as a supplied anatomic observation, not as an independently verified universal cutoff. Exact device-specific suitability and the evidence underlying this close-to-confluence preference require clinical sign-off; no confident clinical inaccuracy is identified from the visible text. Reconstruction is not claimed to be inappropriate in every postoperative stricture.

The named 49-year-old man's prior workup and attendance support a coherent standalone treatment discussion. Attendance does not uniquely name plastic stents because either temporary endoscopic strategy requires follow-up. The parallel ERCP labels provide no grammar or length shortcut. Benign postoperative stricture treatment is high yield, although this particular confluence distinction is more specialized than the core recognition concept.
suggestions: Strengthen the post-answer teaching by explaining the anatomic consequence of the short cuff: a covered stent extending across the confluence may compromise drainage of a hepatic branch. Have the clinician verify the exact wording and its applicability to the intended device context; do not turn the supplied 4 mm observation into an unsupported universal threshold.
